note.text: A prefix attaches before a base, while a suffix attaches after it. Either can affect meaning, and suffixes can change word class. Unhappy uses a negative prefix; helpful uses a suffix to form an adjective. Not every visible letter sequence is a productive affix. Synonyms have related meanings in context, while antonyms oppose meanings on a relevant scale. A word may have several senses, so neither a prefix nor a dictionary synonym permits every possible substitution.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain word formation and preserve contextual meaning when replacing a word. Builds on: context clues and idioms. Leads to: accurate editing of environmental and formal writing.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original model: help, helpful and unhelpful belong to a word family. A calm room may be described as peaceful; an open door contrasts with a closed door. Replacing peaceful with an unrelated look-alike word would not preserve the description. A change of suffix must still fit the required grammatical position.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Find the base, identify the added part and check the resulting word in its sentence. For synonyms and antonyms, preserve the relevant sense and grammatical construction. Verify unfamiliar forms rather than adding un- or -ness to every word mechanically.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: A prefix always follows its base. Correction: Its position is before the base.
Every suffix leaves word class unchanged. Correction: Suffixes can alter class as well as meaning.
A synonym must fit every possible sense of a word. Correction: Related meanings remain context-dependent.
Antonyms are defined only by similar spelling. Correction: The opposition is semantic, not merely visual.
